case.question: How can I connect with my newborn during feeding?
case.expected_behaviour: Gentle age-suitable interaction, without feeding-treatment advice.

retrieved.text: COMMUNICATE Look into baby’s eyes and talk to your baby. When you are breastfeeding is a good time. Even a newborn baby sees your face and hears your voice.

retrieved.text: BREASTFEEDING Newborn upto 1 week • Immediately after birth, put the baby on skin-to-skin contact with the mother for at least one hour. • Initiate breastfeeding within the first hour after birth. Give your baby colostrum (the first yellowish, clear, whitish milk). It protects the baby from many illnesses. • Breastfeed on demand (day and night, as often as the baby wants) at least 8 times in 24 hours. Frequent feeding produces more milk. • If the baby is small (low birth weight - <2500g), feed at least every 2 to 3 hours. Wake the baby for feeding after 3 hours, if baby does not wake self. • DO NOT give other foods. Breast milk is all your baby needs.

records.answer:
Feeding time offers a wonderful opportunity to connect with your newborn. Here are gentle ways to bond while you feed:

Look directly into your baby's eyes and talk or sing softly. Hearing your voice and seeing your face helps your newborn become familiar with you. 

Describe what you are doing or simply chat in a calm, soothing tone. 

Make gentle, unhurried sounds and pause to watch your baby's cues and responses. 

Always keep your baby's head and neck fully supported in a comfortable, safe hold while feeding exclusively with breast milk or infant formula.

case.question: What can I say to my newborn during a bath?
case.expected_behaviour: Simple communication without implying independent bathing.

retrieved.text: A full bath means gently lowering your baby's body into a baby bath or bowl, while supporting their head and shoulders and keeping their head above water. In the first weeks, top and tailing means using warm water to wash the face, neck, hands and bottom rather than putting your baby in a bath. Talk gently while washing so they hear your familiar voice. Never leave your baby alone in a bath, even briefly.

retrieved.text: Support your baby's head and shoulders, keep their head above water, and wash gently without splashing. Never leave a baby alone in a bath, even briefly. Lift them out carefully and pat the skin folds dry.

retrieved.text: Prepare towels, clean clothes, and a nappy before bathing. Keep the room warm, mix the water well, and check it is not hot or cold before putting your baby in. Stay with your baby throughout.

records.answer:
During a bath or top-and-tailing wash, you can talk gently to your newborn so they hear your familiar voice. You might describe what you are doing in a soft, reassuring tone, such as gently telling them it is time to wash their face or warm hands, or simply whisper soothing words and hum quietly. Your calm, familiar voice helps comfort them.

Always keep your baby's head and neck firmly supported while holding them, and never leave your baby alone in water or near a bath, even for a brief moment.

case.question: What simple play can I do with my newborn?
case.expected_behaviour: Newborn-suitable actions; no older-child tasks.

retrieved.text: PLAY Provide ways for your baby to see, hear, move arms and legs freely, and touch you. Gently soothe, stroke and hold your child. Skin to skin is good.
retrieved.title: birth up to 1 week: play
retrieved.source_title: Care for Child Development: Counselling Cards

retrieved.text: How to use these activities • Playtime is very important, play is how young children learn. • The activities are things you can do at home with your child. • First we talk about things that you can do every day to help your children feel safe and happy. • Then play activities are shown by age group, for example 6 to 8 months. Pick the ones for how old your child is. • Try doing one activity playing with objects every day and another one with talking or singing. • You may need to use one or two objects in your home. If you do not have them, see if you can think of something else to use, or just choose another activity. • Let your child play with the objects first. Then show him the activity. If he does not want to do it, that’s okay. Let him play how he wants and try the activity again later. • For a sample of parenting videos that you could use as a guide see link and password in publication available here: https://publications.iadb.org/en/parenting-programme-health-centres- what-you-do-baby-really-matters-implementation-manual • Make time for play every day. Have fun!
retrieved.title: How to use play activities

retrieved.text: When babies explore objects during play and learning, keep small toys, coins and batteries out of reach because they may put objects in their mouths. Keep blind cords and drawstrings out of reach too. Make the surroundings safer rather than relying on watching alone.
retrieved.title: Choking, strangulation and suffocation: exploration and toys
retrieved.source_title: UNICEF: How to babyproof your home

records.answer:
At this newborn stage, play is all about gentle connection and helping your baby experience the world safely. You can:

• Provide ways for your baby to see and hear you by talking softly or singing near them.
• Allow your baby to move their arms and legs freely during quiet alert times.
• Offer gentle touch by stroking their skin and keeping them close with skin-to-skin contact.
• Gently soothe and hold your child, always keeping their head and neck fully supported.

Watch your baby's cues for tiredness, and keep all small items, cords, and strings completely out of reach to maintain a safe environment.

records.answer:
Dressing a newborn can be a gentle, bonding routine. Because a newborn's neck and head are very floppy and lack muscle control, always keep their head and neck fully supported as you move or lift them. 

Choose a warm, flat surface, and lay out the fresh clothes ahead of time so everything is within easy reach. Gather the fabric gently and slide your hand through the sleeve or pants leg first, then catch your baby’s hand or foot to guide it through smoothly, avoiding any forceful pulling on their delicate limbs. Keep the room comfortably warm to prevent chilling. 

As you dress your baby, spend quiet face-to-face time talking to them in a soft, soothing voice. Describe your actions as you go, using repeated, simple phrases like taking socks off or putting sleeves on, and pause gently to watch for their responses.

records.answer: Yes, you can share a book with your newborn. Hold your baby comfortably in your arms or lap, making sure to keep their head and neck fully supported at all times. Look at a picture book together, even if you only look at a single page. Follow your baby's cues and interest, pointing to objects, naming them, or making gentle sounds rather than trying to read a whole story. If you do not have a book on hand, you can simply tell your baby a story; hearing the sound of your voice will make your baby feel happy. You can also engage in quiet turn-taking by making gentle caregiver sounds, pausing, and watching your baby's facial expressions and responses without requiring any action in return.

records.answer:
It is wonderful that your newborn makes little sounds when you talk to them. Newborns hear your voice and often respond with tiny sounds, sighs, or murmurs. 

You can gently talk, sing, or whisper to your baby while looking into their eyes, such as during feeding time while always keeping their head and neck fully supported. When your baby makes a noise, give them your attention and respond softly. You can make a gentle sound, pause to watch your baby's facial expressions or movements, and wait to see if they make another sound, without requiring any specific response. 

Always ensure your baby is comfortable and supported safely during all interactions. If you ever have worries about your newborn's hearing or responses, consult a qualified health worker in Kenya for guidance.

records.answer:
Prepare towels, clean clothes, and a nappy before you begin, and make sure the room is comfortably warm. Check that the bath water is warm, not hot or cold, by mixing it well. 

Support your 3-month-old baby's head and shoulders securely, keeping their head well above the water at all times. Wash them gently without splashing, and remember never to leave your baby alone in the bath, even for a brief moment. When finished, lift them out carefully and pat their skin folds dry.

records.answer:
To encourage your three-month-old baby to notice sounds during play, you can try these simple activities:

* Talk softly, coo, and smile while looking directly into your baby's eyes.
* Make a new sound, then wait patiently to see if your baby responds or makes a noise back.
* Describe what you are doing around the house or talk about things your baby is looking at.
* Sing gentle songs or shake a soft-sounding rattle gently out of direct sight to see if your baby turns toward the noise.

Keep sound levels comfortable and watch your baby for signs of becoming overwhelmed, such as turning away or crying. If you ever have concerns about how your baby responds to sounds, consult a healthcare professional in Kenya for guidance.

records.answer:
Transform dressing time into a special bonding moment by turning it into a conversation. 

First, spend precious face-to-face time leaning over your 3-month-old baby, making eye contact and smiling warmly as you begin. 

Second, describe your actions step-by-step using repeated simple phrases, such as "off go the socks" or "here comes the soft shirt." 

Third, repeat familiar words and sounds, pausing to listen and respond when your baby coos or gazes back at you. 

Fourth, sing a gentle, repetitive song while guiding garments over your baby's limbs. 

As a precaution, always keep one hand gently on your baby's body to prevent rolling off high surfaces during dressing.

It is wonderful that you are sharing books with your three-month-old! Looking briefly is very typical at this stage. You can support your baby's developing vision and attention with a few simple steps:

* Share pictures with your baby, even if you look at only one page.
* Follow your baby's interest by pointing to images, naming things, or making fun sounds rather than trying to read a whole story.
* Choose high-contrast books with bold black-and-white patterns or bright primary colors, which are easier for young eyes to focus on.
* Keep sessions short and stop if your baby looks away, fusses, or seems tired.

Always ensure books are clean and safe for your baby to look at while you hold them securely.

records.answer:
When your three-month-old makes a sound and then pauses, it is a wonderful moment of early communication. They are learning how conversations work by taking turns, even before they use words. 

You can encourage this natural back-and-forth interaction by following these steps:
* Face your baby and smile when they make a sound, showing them you are listening.
* Repeat the exact sound back to them clearly and warmly.
* Wait patiently to see if they respond or make another sound. 
* Keep the interaction gentle and stop if your baby looks away, yawns, or seems tired so they do not become overstimulated. 

Enjoy talking and listening together as they explore their voice!

records.answer:
Bath time is a wonderful opportunity to help your six-month-old learn new words through simple, engaging play. 

You can support your baby's language development with these easy steps:
* Talk directly to your baby and have fun together while splashing water gently.
* Use a plastic cup or container to scoop water, and say the words "full" and "empty" as you fill and empty it.
* Name body parts as you gently wash them, such as "tummy," "toes," or "hands."
* Introduce floating toys and describe their actions, saying words like "float" or "down."

Always support your baby's head and shoulders, keep their head well above the water, and never leave your baby alone in the bath, even for a single second.

It is wonderful that your six-month-old watches you during dressing. This is a great opportunity to support their early language and social development.

* Talk to your baby about what you are doing, such as saying, "Let's put on your shirt."
* Name your baby's body parts as you dress them, like asking them to "Hold up your arm."
* Play simple finger or toe games together, such as reciting "This little piggy."

Keep clothing comfortable, loose-fitting, and suited to the weather to make dressing smooth and easy for your baby.

records.answer: Share simple picture books with your 6-month-old by holding the book where they can see it and describing what the pictures show. Choose sturdy board books with bright, clear images. Let your baby explore the book at their own pace, allowing them to move through pages quickly or linger on a favourite one, and notice which pictures catch their attention. Try textured books so your baby can safely feel different surfaces while listening to your voice. Connect the pictured objects to familiar real things around you, like pointing from a picture of a cup to an actual cup. Always supervise your baby closely during book time, as 6-month-old babies frequently explore objects by putting them straight into their mouths.

records.answer:
It is wonderful when your 6-month-old starts copying sounds. This back-and-forth interaction builds early communication skills. You can encourage this progress with a few simple steps:

- Hold your baby close and look directly into their eyes while talking or making playful sounds.
- Listen carefully to the sounds your baby makes, then repeat one of them back and wait to see if they respond.
- Share a simple picture book together, describing the pictures or reading a textured book so your baby can feel the pages.
- Take turns making sounds or splashing gently during bath time, pausing to give your baby a chance to answer.

Ensure your baby is seated securely or held safely during these activities to prevent slips or falls. Every baby develops at their own pace, so enjoy these engaging moments together.

records.answer:
Mealtimes are a wonderful opportunity to build language skills with your twelve-month-old. 

* Talk through the meal by naming the foods, colors, and textures on their plate, keeping sentences simple.
* Pause after asking a question or making a comment to give your baby time to process and attempt a response or gesture.
* Respond enthusiastically to any sounds, pointing, or words your baby uses, repeating them back correctly.
* Eat together whenever possible, making eye contact and showing enjoyment of the food to model conversation.

Always supervise your baby closely while eating, keeping food cut into small, manageable pieces to reduce the risk of choking.

records.answer:
It is wonderful that your twelve-month-old is pointing during bath time! This is a great opportunity to connect and communicate. As you wash, name the body parts you are cleaning, such as your baby's arm, leg, or tummy, and respond when they point or try to help. You can also name the objects you use or invite your child to point to what to wash next. 

While enjoying this interactive play, always stay within arm's reach and keep your full attention on your child, as a small amount of water can still be dangerous. Never leave a young child unattended, even briefly, and empty the tub right after use.

records.answer:
Practising taking turns with a 12-month-old helps build early social skills through simple back-and-forth games. 

Try these engaging ways to play together:
* Practise taking turns by pulling clothing items out of a cloth bag together, naming each item as you play.
* Roll a soft ball back and forth, gently encouraging your child to roll it back to you.
* Take turns dropping blocks into a container, cheering when each piece goes in.
* Alternate turns building a tall tower with large blocks and knocking it down together.

Choose toys sized too large to swallow to prevent choking hazards during play. Stay close and supervise your child actively throughout the activity.

Dressing your 12-month-old is a great opportunity to connect and help them learn new words. You can turn this routine into an interactive game by inviting your child to help out, such as by offering an arm or a leg when asked. 

As you help your toddler get dressed, describe each action using simple words. For example, talk about an arm going into a shirt or name body parts as you go, saying things like, "Let’s put on your blue t-shirt," or "Put the sock on your foot." 

Keep clothing items simple and loose-fitting to make dressing smoother, and always ensure small items like buttons or snaps are secure so they do not pose a choking hazard. Never leave your child unattended on an elevated surface like a bed or changing table while getting them dressed.

records.answer:
It is wonderful that your twelve-month-old is pointing at pictures in books. This is a lovely way to share reading time together. 

To encourage this interaction, you can sit with your child on your lap and follow their interests by looking at the pictures they point to. Describe what they notice using simple words for objects and actions, make fun sounds, and give your toddler time to turn the pages themselves. Avoid rushing through the story, and keep book-sharing relaxed and engaging. 

For safety during reading, choose sturdy board books with rounded corners to prevent paper cuts or injury, and always supervise your child closely with books to ensure they do not tear and mouth small pieces.

Following your 12-month-old's interests during play helps build a strong connection and encourages communication. Here are practical ways to join in:

• Observe what captures your child's attention—whether they are staring at a toy, pointing at a picture, or exploring an object—and join in with that exact activity.
• Ask your child simple questions and respond enthusiastically to their babbles and attempts to talk, showing that you are listening.
• Sit close and engage in shared play, such as simple hiding games or handing toys back and forth.
• Show and talk about things around you, including nature, everyday objects, and pictures in books.

When playing together, always stay close and supervise actively to ensure small toys or objects do not pose a choking hazard.

records.answer:
At 12 months old, every child reaches developmental milestones at their own unique pace, and there is a wide range of typical progress. Rather than following a fixed schedule, your baby may be working on pulling up to stand, taking their first tentative steps, waving bye-bye, or saying a few simple words like mama or dada. 

To support your twelve-month-old's growth, encourage exploration in a safe, child-proofed space by removing small objects, covering electrical outlets, and keeping sharp corners padded to prevent injuries. 

If you ever have specific questions or concerns about your baby's development, it is best to consult a qualified health worker for guidance tailored to your child.

Mealtimes are a wonderful opportunity to connect and support your two-year-old's communication skills.

Use a variety of names, action words, and descriptions—such as cup, drinking, or cold—to keep the conversation flowing. Keep conversations relaxed and positive without pressuring your child to eat more than they want. Always supervise your child closely while they are eating to prevent choking.

records.answer:
Bath time is a wonderful opportunity to build language skills with your twenty-four-month-old. You can talk about body parts by naming fingers, toes, and arms as you gently wash them. Introduce objects used during the routine, such as the soap and towels. Describe the water using lively action words like splash, pour, or drip, and talk about whether the water feels warm or cool. You might also count splashing drops or talk about washing a toy. 

As a safety precaution, always stay within arm's reach and keep your full attention on your child during bath time, as young children can slip or submerge in very little water.

records.answer:
At twenty-four months, children love imitating everyday actions and using their imaginations. Here are some pretend play ideas you can try together:

- Act out a simple story using a soft toy or teddy, and let your toddler lead the game while you talk about the pretend actions.
- Play house or cooking by pretending to feed dolls or stirring pretend food in a bowl together.
- Play doctor or nurse by gently checking a stuffed animal's heartbeat or putting a pretend plaster on a toy.
- Put on a few old clothes, hats, or shoes for a simple dress-up game.

Always supervise play closely to ensure small toy accessories or props do not present a choking hazard.

records.answer:
At 24 months, your toddler can actively join in during dressing by helping with simple, playful tasks rather than dressing independently. Try these ideas:

* Offer two choices of shirts or shorts and let your child pick what to wear.
* Ask your child to push their arms through sleeves or push their feet into shoes.
* Have your child help pull up elastic-waist trousers or pull off socks.
* Let your child help sort clothes or place dirty items into a basket.

Keep dressing playful and acknowledge their help with cheerful encouragement. Ensure any buttons, zippers, or small clothing accessories are kept out of reach to avoid choking hazards.

records.answer:
To make picture-book time more interactive with your twenty-four-month-old, follow their interests rather than asking lots of questions. Try these engaging steps:

* Add fun sounds for animals, vehicles, or objects in the story.
* Act out character actions, such as clapping or waving.
* Talk about the pictures together, naming what you see.
* Let your toddler turn the paper pages themselves to help them stay involved.

Keep book-sharing relaxed and fun, stopping if your child loses interest.

When your twenty-four-month-old brings you a toy and waits, it is a wonderful opportunity to connect and support their social interaction. Share play and conversation by accepting the toy and engaging with it together. You can hand toys back and forth between each other or roll a ball back and forth. 

As a simple precaution, ensure any toys or items shared during play are clean and free of small, detachable parts that could pose a choking hazard. This interactive sharing helps build early communication and social skills as your child learns the back-and-forth rhythm of conversation and play.

records.answer:
While there is no guaranteed way to maximize intelligence, you can strongly support your 24-month-old's cognitive and social growth through everyday interactions. 

Here are four ways to help your child thrive:
1. Talk and sing together frequently, naming objects around your home to build vocabulary.
2. Read colorful picture books daily, asking simple questions about the pictures.
3. Encourage imaginative play using everyday items like safe kitchen containers.
4. Provide opportunities to explore safely outdoors under your close supervision to protect against hazards.

Every child develops at their own unique pace. If you ever have specific concerns about your child's learning or developmental milestones, consult a qualified healthcare worker.

records.answer:
At this earliest stage, feeding means exclusive breast milk or infant formula, given with careful support for your newborn's head and neck. 

Even though newborns do not yet speak, smile, or coo on demand, you can encourage early connection during feeding with gentle, loving communication:
* Hold your baby close and speak or sing softly in a gentle, soothing voice.
* Watch your baby's cues, such as eye movements or settling into your arms, responding warmly when they seem alert.
* Offer soft vocal sounds or gentle words, then pause to watch your baby without expecting an immediate reply. 
* Keep the atmosphere calm and unhurried so your baby feels secure. 

Solid foods are not appropriate now and are typically introduced around six months when developmental readiness signs appear, following individual clinician advice.

At this newborn stage, play focuses on gentle connection and communication. You can practise taking turns by using soft caregiver sounds, making eye contact, and pausing to watch your baby's cues to see how they respond, without requiring them to give a specific reaction. 

To keep your newborn safe, always ensure their head and neck are fully supported when you hold or position them. You can talk softly, pause to let your baby take in the sound, and then gently speak again when they look your way. Watch closely for signs that your baby is getting tired or overwhelmed, such as turning away or fussing, and give them quiet time to rest.

records.answer:
At 3 months old, your baby's nutrition relies exclusively on breast milk or infant formula. Solid foods and seated mealtime activities are not introduced at this age. Discuss the introduction of solids around six months with your healthcare provider based on your baby's individual developmental readiness. 

For now, continue to feed your baby exclusively with breast milk or infant formula on demand. If you have any specific questions about feeding frequency, milk intake, or your baby's growth, consult a local healthcare professional in Kenya for personalized guidance.

records.answer:
Night waking is very common for a six-month-old, as babies this age often wake for feeds or comfort and are going through rapid developmental changes. 

To help encourage better sleep patterns, you can establish a simple, calming bedtime routine. Keep a familiar sequence each night, such as putting on clean night clothes, sharing a quiet cuddle or lullaby, and reducing excitement before sleep. 

Ensure your baby sleeps safely on their back on a firm, flat surface with no loose blankets, pillows, or toys in the cot to reduce the risk of sudden infant death. Sleep patterns vary widely, and a routine does not guarantee uninterrupted sleep. If you have ongoing concerns about your baby's sleep or health, consult a local health worker.

records.answer:
Happy first birthday to your little one! At 12 months, you can focus on supporting exciting new milestones in several simple ways:

1. Communication: Talk with your toddler during feeding, bathing, and play. Ask simple questions, respond to their attempts to speak, and name what they are doing.
2. Play and thinking: Try putting suitable objects into a container and taking them out, copying gestures, or looking for hidden objects. Always supervise closely with small objects to prevent choking.
3. Movement: Allow supervised movement on a flat surface, keeping the area clear of sharp edges or hazards to ensure safety.

Children vary widely in their development. If you ever notice a loss of previously acquired skills or have specific concerns about your child's progress, discuss them with a pediatrician or local health worker.

records.answer: It is common for an 18-month-old to hesitate with new textures. Introduce new foods gradually by placing a tiny taste alongside familiar favorites without pressure. Let your child explore food with their hands to become comfortable with how it feels. Talk about the food during meals, describing its color and taste to make it inviting. Always stay with your child while they eat and encourage them to sit still to prevent choking. If feeding difficulties persist or you have nutrition concerns, consult a health worker.

records.answer:
It is common for a 6-month-old to spit up small amounts of milk after feeding, but it is important to watch for other signs. To help reduce spit-up, try keeping your baby upright for about twenty to thirty minutes after a feed, and avoid bouncing or playing too actively right away. Burping your baby frequently during feeds can also help release trapped air. 

If your baby is starting on soft foods alongside continued breastfeeding or other milk feeds, introduce them patiently. However, contact a health worker promptly if your baby has forceful or projectile vomiting, spits up green or bloody fluid, cries persistently in pain, refuses feeds, or is not gaining weight well.

records.answer:
To help soothe and heal your 18-month-old's nappy rash, follow these gentle steps:

Change nappies frequently to keep your baby's skin clean and dry. Gently clean the area with warm water and a soft cloth or cotton wool, avoiding harsh scented wipes that can sting. Pat the skin completely dry rather than rubbing. 

Give your toddler some daily "nappy-free time" to let fresh air circulate against the skin, laying them on a waterproof mat or towel. Apply a thick layer of a protective barrier cream, such as zinc oxide, at every nappy change to shield the skin from moisture. 

If the rash does not improve after a few days, appears raw, or if your baby develops a fever, consult a healthcare provider or visit your local health facility in Kenya for professional assessment and advice.

Your child's recorded age is 9.0 months. Kenya's routine visits around your child's age:
- 9 months: Measles-rubella (MR) 1, IPV 2 and typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV); malaria vaccine 3 in eligible programme areas, and yellow fever vaccine in designated risk areas.
- 18 months: MR 2.

Malaria and yellow fever vaccines are not offered routinely in every area. Ask your vaccination clinic to confirm local eligibility and the malaria vaccine product in use.

Take your child's Mother and Child Health booklet or vaccination record to the clinic. These routine ages do not show which doses your child has already received or is due for; the clinic needs their record to confirm the next appointment.

records.answer:
At around 6 weeks old, breastfeed your baby on demand, both day and night, as often as they want. This typically means at least 8 times in every 24-hour period. 

Watch for early signs of hunger, such as fussing, sucking on hands, moving the lips, or opening the mouth, rather than waiting for crying. Frequent feeding helps ensure your baby gets enough milk and helps maintain your milk supply. Breast milk provides all the nutrition an infant needs at this stage; do not give other foods or fluids. 

Monitor your baby's wet nappies to help gauge whether they are feeding well. If you have any concerns about feeding patterns or your baby's weight gain, consult a healthcare worker in Kenya for guidance.

records.answer:
Talk gently to your newborn during a bath so they hear your familiar voice. You can use a calm, soothing tone to describe what you are doing, such as gently washing their face, neck, hands, and bottom with warm water, or simply whisper gentle words of comfort. Speak in soft, musical rhythms or sing a quiet lullaby while maintaining a gentle, reassuring sound. 

Always keep the room warm and never leave your baby alone in a bath, even briefly. Support your baby's head and shoulders securely while keeping their head well above water, and ensure all items like towels and clean clothes are prepared beforehand.

records.answer:
Newborns do not follow a fixed schedule for learning new skills on a specific day, as early development varies greatly for every baby. Instead of a set lesson plan, tomorrow will be filled with quiet adjustments to the world outside the womb, sleeping, feeding exclusively on breast milk or infant formula, and responding to gentle care. 

You can support your baby's early experiences by talking softly while holding them close, ensuring their head and neck are always fully supported. Describe what you are doing during diaper changes and feeding times, and gently watch their responses without expecting any specific reaction. Every newborn develops at their own pace, so simply focus on comforting, feeding, and responding to your baby's needs.

Keep feeding interactions calm and unhurried to help your baby feel secure and connected.

records.answer:
Spitting up small amounts of milk after feeding is common. To help manage this, feed smaller amounts more frequently and keep your baby in an upright position during and for about 30 minutes after a meal. Avoid bouncing or active play right after feeding to let the stomach settle. Ensure your baby is held close during feeding, looking at you while you talk or sing. 

Watch for signs that need medical attention. Seek advice from a health worker promptly if your baby has forceful or projectile vomiting, green vomit, blood in the spit-up, poor weight gain, persistent crying during or after feeds, or breathing difficulties.

records.answer:
To help soothe a nappy rash, change your baby's nappy frequently to keep their skin dry and clean. Gently clean the area with plain water or a soft, damp cloth, avoiding harsh wipes that might sting, and pat the skin completely dry instead of rubbing. Whenever possible, let your baby spend some time each day without a nappy to let the skin air out. You can also apply a thick layer of a protective barrier cream, such as zinc oxide, at every nappy change. 

Consult a health worker if the rash does not improve after a few days, looks severe, starts blistering, or if your baby develops a fever.

retrieved.text: Looking after yourself It is important to take care of yourself. Being kind and patient with yourself will help you stay calm and be kind and patient with others. Here are some things you can try: • Keep in touch with family and friends, with a phone call if you can’t visit. • Try and rest when your child is resting, and try to get enough sleep at night. • If you feel stressed or angry take some long deep breaths. • Take short breaks. Get a glass of water or cup of tea and sit somewhere to drink it. Find things that help you relax and smile, maybe a funny TV show. • Limit how much you listen to the news if it is upsetting. • Tell family members or friends how you are feeling. Don’t be afraid to ask them for help so that you can have some time for yourself. • Before you go to sleep try and remember something your child did today that made you smile or feel good. Think of things that went well or people who were kind to you.

records.answer: Try offering a gentle change of position, such as holding your baby upright against your chest with their head and neck fully supported, or gently rocking them in a quiet, dimly lit room. You can also try swaddling your baby snugly in a light blanket to help them feel secure, while ensuring they are placed safely on their back for sleep and cannot overheat. If crying is persistent, unusual, or accompanied by other symptoms like fever or poor feeding, seek advice from a health worker.

records.answer:
Offer nutritious family foods cut into safe, manageable pieces to prevent choking. Try soft-cooked vegetable sticks, small pieces of tender meat or beans, and mashed or sliced fruit. 

Include a variety of textures and food groups across meals, allowing self-feeding with fingers or a spoon. Always supervise closely while eating, ensure your child sits upright during meals, and avoid hard, round, or sticky foods like whole grapes, nuts, or hard sweets that pose choking hazards. Offer water in an open cup or small beaker alongside meals.

Add MNPs 7-8 months Mashed family foods, by 8 months your baby can begin eating finger food. Frequent breast feeds Feed your child 3 times (3 meals) Increase amount gradually to half (½) cup (250ml cup). Frequent breast feeds, feed your baby 5 times, (3 meals, 2 snacks) Give your child 1 cup (250ml cup). retrieved.text: 1 WEEK UP TO 6 MONTHS • Breastfeed as often as the child wants. Look for signs of hunger, (fuss, sucking/moving lips, opening mouth, making sounds, sticking out the tongue, putting hands in his mouth, making rapid eye movement before his/her eyes are open, baby may cry) • Breastfeed on demand (day and night, as often as the baby wants) at least 8 times in 24 hours. Frequent feeding produces more milk. • Breast milk is all your baby needs. • DO NOT give other foods or fluids

records.answer: Feed your baby on demand, both day and night, aiming for at least 8 times in 24 hours. Watch for hunger cues such as sucking or moving their lips, opening their mouth, making sounds, sticking out the tongue, or putting hands in their mouth. Frequent feeding helps produce more milk and ensures they get enough nutrition. At this stage, breast milk is all your baby needs; do not give other foods or fluids. Keep track of their wet nappies to help gauge how well they are feeding.

records.answer:
Feed your baby exclusively breast milk or infant formula, keeping their head and neck fully supported throughout. Mealtimes offer a wonderful opportunity for early bonding and communication. 

* Speak softly in a gentle, calming tone while feeding, as your baby is learning to recognize your voice.
* Pause naturally during the feed to watch your baby's cues, such as eye movements or changes in breathing, allowing a gentle rhythm of connection without requiring a response.
* Gently stroke your baby's cheek or hold their tiny hand to offer comforting reassurance.
* Make soft, responsive vocal sounds when your baby makes eye contact, sharing a quiet moment together.

retrieved.text: How to use these activities • Playtime is very important, play is how young children learn. • The activities are things you can do at home with your child. • First we talk about things that you can do every day to help your children feel safe and happy. • Then play activities are shown by age group, for example 6 to 8 months. Pick the ones for how old your child is. • Try doing one activity playing with objects every day and another one with talking or singing. • You may need to use one or two objects in your home. If you do not have them, see if you can think of something else to use, or just choose another activity. • Let your child play with the objects first. Then show him the activity. If he does not want to do it, that’s okay. Let him play how he wants and try the activity again later. • For a sample of parenting videos that you could use as a guide see link and password in publication available here: https://publications.iadb.org/en/parenting-programme-health-centres- what-you-do-baby-really-matters-implementation-manual • Make time for play every day. Have fun!

Enjoy calm moments together, keeping play very simple and restful.

records.answer:
Prepare soft family foods cut into small, easy-to-manage pieces that your toddler can pick up, chew, and swallow comfortably. Good options include mashed or lightly cooked vegetables, small pieces of tender meat, soft ripe fruits, and well-cooked grains or pulses. 

Always stay with your child while they are eating to help prevent choking, and encourage them to sit quietly rather than running around with food. Avoid offering whole nuts, hard sweets, or foods that are difficult to chew safely.

records.answer: Try offering simple finger foods like small cubes of soft cheese, well-cooked pasta shapes, or small steamed broccoli florets that your toddler can easily pick up. You can also try offering nutrient-dense options such as scrambled eggs, well-mashed beans, or small pieces of soft-baked fish. Cut all foods into small, manageable pieces to help prevent choking, and always stay close while they eat.

records.answer: Offer finger foods like soft-cooked carrot batons, small pieces of ripe banana, or well-cooked pasta shapes that your toddler can easily pick up and hold. Let your child practise using a spoon with mashed foods, keeping meals simple and manageable. Cut round foods like grapes or cherry tomatoes into small, lengthwise quarters to reduce the risk of choking. Always stay close and supervise your toddler actively while eating, and encourage them to sit quietly at the table rather than walking or running around with food.

conversation_context.text: 18 months

Prepare soft family foods cut into small, easy-to-manage pieces that your toddler can pick up, chew, and swallow comfortably. Good options include mashed or lightly cooked vegetables, small pieces of tender meat, soft ripe fruits, and well-cooked grains or pulses. 

Always stay with your child while they are eating to help prevent choking, and encourage them to sit quietly rather than running around with food. Avoid offering whole nuts, hard sweets, or foods that are difficult to chew safely.
conversation_context.caregiver_request: What food can I make for my toddler?

conversation_context.text: What else can I try?

Try offering simple finger foods like small cubes of soft cheese, well-cooked pasta shapes, or small steamed broccoli florets that your toddler can easily pick up. You can also try offering nutrient-dense options such as scrambled eggs, well-mashed beans, or small pieces of soft-baked fish. Cut all foods into small, manageable pieces to help prevent choking, and always stay close while they eat.

records.answer: Keep your baby's sleeping space in the same room as you for both daytime and night-time sleep, placing them on their back on a firm, flat surface to help keep them safe. Dim the lights and keep nighttime interactions quiet and calm to help your baby learn the difference between day and night. Offer frequent feeds of breast milk or infant formula as needed, keeping your baby's head and neck fully supported while holding and feeding. If you need help with sleep concerns or routines, speak to a health professional.

retrieved.text: When a baby has started solid foods, consider food size, shape and texture. Stay with the child during eating and encourage sitting still rather than running around with food. Do not offer whole nuts or hard sweets to young children.

records.answer:
Offer varied family foods prepared so your child can easily manage them. Here are options you can make:

* Soft-cooked vegetables and ripe fruit
* Well-cooked eggs
* Mashed beans or lentils
* Tender meat or fish with all bones completely removed

Chop, mash, or soften foods so they are easy to eat, and let your child practise self-feeding without pressure. Always keep your child sitting upright and stay close while they eat. Avoid whole nuts and other hard choking hazards.

Promptly change wet or soiled nappies and clean the skin gently using plain water or fragrance-free, alcohol-free wipes, patting dry rather than rubbing. Here are some things you can try: • Keep in touch with family and friends, with a phone call if you can’t visit. • Try and rest when your child is resting, and try to get enough sleep at night. • If you feel stressed or angry take some long deep breaths. • Take short breaks. Get a glass of water or cup of tea and sit somewhere to drink it. Find things that help you relax and smile, maybe a funny TV show. • Limit how much you listen to the news if it is upsetting. • Tell family members or friends how you are feeling. Don’t be afraid to ask them for help so that you can have some time for yourself. • Before you go to sleep try and remember something your child did today that made you smile or feel good. Think of things that went well or people who were kind to you.

records.answer: Create a predictable, calming bedtime sequence each night. Start by reducing exciting play and loud noises about thirty minutes before sleep. Guide your child through a quiet wind-down by changing into night clothes, dimming the lights, and sharing a gentle story together. Keep nighttime interactions quiet and low-key if your child wakes up. Ensure the sleep space remains safe by keeping heavy blankets, pillows, and toys out of the cot to lower the risk of suffocation. Remember that sleep patterns vary naturally, and a routine helps cue sleep but does not promise an uninterrupted night.

records.answer:
Hold your baby close and maintain gentle eye contact during feeding to build a strong connection. 

Try these simple conversation ideas:
• Talk about the food itself, naming the items or describing how they taste.
• Describe what you are doing together, such as saying, "Now it is time for another spoonful."
• Respond to any sounds, babbles, or gestures your baby makes, taking turns just like in a real conversation.
• Notice what catches your baby's interest around the room and talk about those things.

Always keep feeding calm and unhurried, stopping promptly if your baby shows signs of being full or upset.

records.answer:
Focus on communication, play, and exploration as your child reaches this milestone. 

* Talk and listen: Ask simple questions, respond to your child's attempts to speak, and point out and talk about pictures, nature, and everyday objects.
* Explore and discover: Try putting suitable objects into a container and taking them out together, or play peek-a-boo games by hiding objects and looking for them. Ensure any small items used for play are large enough not to be choking hazards.
* Copy and learn: Encourage your child to copy simple gestures like waving goodbye or clapping. Offer gentle help with new tasks, gradually reducing your assistance as your child gains confidence. 
* Support movement: Create a safe, uncluttered space for cruising along furniture or practicing early steps, keeping sharp corners and stairs safely blocked.

case.question: Which vaccines are scheduled in Kenya at this age?

records.answer:
Your child's recorded age is 9.0 months. Kenya's routine visits around your child's age:
- 9 months: Measles-rubella (MR) 1, IPV 2 and typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV); malaria vaccine 3 in eligible programme areas, and yellow fever vaccine in designated risk areas.
- 18 months: MR 2.

Malaria and yellow fever vaccines are not offered routinely in every area. Ask your vaccination clinic to confirm local eligibility and the malaria vaccine product in use.

Take your child's Mother and Child Health booklet or vaccination record to the clinic. These routine ages do not show which doses your child has already received or is due for; the clinic needs their record to confirm the next appointment.

records.answer:
Promptly change wet or dirty nappies, and clean the skin gently using water or fragrance-free, alcohol-free wipes before drying it thoroughly. Give the skin some time without a nappy when practical, and avoid tight clothing, irritating soaps, and talcum powder, as these can increase irritation. case.question: How can I make bedtime calmer for my child?

retrieved.text: A simple calming bedtime routine may include clean night clothes, a story, a cuddle, and a lullaby. Reduce excitement before bed and keep a familiar sequence as your child grows. Sleep patterns vary; a routine does not guarantee uninterrupted sleep.
retrieved.title: Establishing a bedtime routine
retrieved.source_title: NHS: Helping your baby to sleep

retrieved.text: Have Routines • Routines help children feel safe. • Have a routine for bedtime. For example, bath, cuddle and look at a book together or sing a song. • Try to also have a routine for the day, such as resting and eating meals at around the same time each day, it doesn’t matter if you cannot always do this.
retrieved.title: Have routines for your child

retrieved.text: Looking after yourself It is important to take care of yourself. Being kind and patient with yourself will help you stay calm and be kind and patient with others. Here are some things you can try: • Keep in touch with family and friends, with a phone call if you can’t visit. • Try and rest when your child is resting, and try to get enough sleep at night. • If you feel stressed or angry take some long deep breaths. • Take short breaks. Get a glass of water or cup of tea and sit somewhere to drink it. Find things that help you relax and smile, maybe a funny TV show. • Limit how much you listen to the news if it is upsetting. • Tell family members or friends how you are feeling. Don’t be afraid to ask them for help so that you can have some time for yourself. • Before you go to sleep try and remember something your child did today that made you smile or feel good. Think of things that went well or people who were kind to you.
retrieved.title: Looking after yourself as a caregiver

supplied_evidence.text: Keep a familiar, calming bedtime sequence, such as changing into night clothes, sharing a quiet story and dimming the light. Reduce excitement before bed and keep nighttime care quiet. Sleep patterns vary; a routine does not promise an uninterrupted night.

supplied_evidence.source_title: NHS: Helping your baby to sleep

records.answer:
Help create a calmer bedtime by keeping a familiar, soothing sequence every evening. Start by reducing exciting play and loud noises as bedtime approaches. 

Try these practical steps:
1. Change into comfortable night clothes in a quiet room.
2. Dim the lights to signal that sleep is near.
3. Share a quiet story together in a calm, gentle voice.
4. Keep nighttime interactions low-key and quiet if your child wakes up. 

Ensure loose bedding, pillows, and heavy blankets are kept out of the sleeping area to maintain a safe sleep environment. Remember that sleep patterns vary widely, and a routine helps cue sleep but does not promise an uninterrupted night.

records.answer:
Try offering these additional meal ideas:

* Small pieces of soft-cooked ugali served with a mild, vegetable-rich stew
* Thinly sliced soft ripe avocado wedges for easy grabbing
* Soft porridge made from nutrient-dense flours, cooled to a safe temperature
* Small spoonfuls of smooth peanut paste mixed thoroughly into mashed sweet potato

Always keep your child sitting upright during meals, stay close while they eat, and watch carefully to prevent choking. Avoid adding extra salt, sugar, or honey to these dishes.

conversation_context.text: What food can I make for my toddler?

Offer varied family foods prepared so your child can easily manage them. Here are options you can make:

* Soft-cooked vegetables and ripe fruit
* Well-cooked eggs
* Mashed beans or lentils
* Tender meat or fish with all bones completely removed

Chop, mash, or soften foods so they are easy to eat, and let your child practise self-feeding without pressure. Always keep your child sitting upright and stay close while they eat. Avoid whole nuts and other hard choking hazards.

records.answer:
To help reduce spit-up, you can try feeding smaller amounts more frequently, keeping your baby calm and relaxed during feeds to limit air swallowing, and ensuring they wear loose clothing around their tummy without tight waistbands. Always keep your baby upright while awake during and after feeds, but for sleep, continue to place them flat on their back. 

Seek prompt medical assessment if the spitting up is painful or persistent, if there is poor weight gain, or if you notice any new symptoms. Get urgent care immediately if your baby has forceful, green or bloody vomit, cannot keep fluids down, or refuses to feed.

records.answer: You can try ensuring the nappy area is completely dry before putting on a fresh nappy, as trapped moisture can worsen irritation. Applying a thick layer of a protective barrier ointment recommended by your pharmacist at each change can also help shield the skin from wetness. If you use reusable cloth nappies, check that rinsing removes all soap residue, which can sometimes contribute to soreness. Have a health professional assess the skin if the rash persists, worsens, spreads, causes marked discomfort, or appears alongside a fever.

conversation_context.text: My baby has a nappy rash. What can I try?

Promptly change wet or soiled nappies and clean the skin gently using plain water or fragrance-free, alcohol-free wipes, patting dry rather than rubbing. Leave the nappy off for short periods when practical to let the skin breathe, and avoid tight nappies, talcum powder, and scented soaps that can irritate. 

Ask a pharmacist or health professional for a suitable barrier cream or treatment product rather than selecting one yourself. Because rashes cannot be diagnosed through chat, have a health professional assess the skin if the rash persists, worsens, spreads, causes marked discomfort, or appears alongside a fever.

records.answer:
Gently cleanse the nappy area with plain water or fragrance-free, alcohol-free wipes during changes, and pat the skin dry carefully rather than rubbing, which can add friction and irritation. Ensure your baby's skin is completely dry before putting on a fresh nappy. 

If you have already tried these steps and need further ideas, consider switching to a slightly larger nappy size temporarily to reduce friction against the sore skin, and make sure nappy-free time is built into your daily routine so fresh air can reach the area. 

Because rashes cannot be diagnosed through chat, consult a pharmacist or health professional about a suitable barrier product rather than choosing one yourself. Have a health professional assess the skin promptly if the rash persists, worsens, spreads, causes marked discomfort, or appears alongside a fever.

Promptly change wet or soiled nappies and clean the skin gently using plain water or fragrance-free, alcohol-free wipes, patting dry rather than rubbing. Leave the nappy off for short periods when practical to let the skin breathe, and avoid tight nappies, talcum powder, and scented soaps that can irritate. 

Ask a pharmacist or health professional for a suitable barrier cream or treatment product rather than selecting one yourself. Because rashes cannot be diagnosed through chat, have a health professional assess the skin if the rash persists, worsens, spreads, causes marked discomfort, or appears alongside a fever.
